methods.label: Compare truth conditions
methods.explanation:
In mathematical logic, an implication is false only when its hypothesis is true and its conclusion is false. Comparing these false cases lets us test equivalence for every possible combination of facts.

Let \(P\) mean that the elephant has purple eyes, and let \(L\) mean that the pig has a long nose. The original statement is “if \(P\), then not \(L\).” It is false exactly when \(P\) and \(L\) are both true.

Statement III says “if \(L\), then not \(P\).” It has exactly the same false case, so it is equivalent to the original.

Statement IV says “not \(P\), or not \(L\).” An inclusive “or” is false only when both alternatives are false. Thus IV is also false exactly when \(P\) and \(L\) are both true, establishing equivalence.

To rule out I and II, take \(P\) false and \(L\) true. The original implication is true because its hypothesis is false. But I and II each have a true hypothesis and a false conclusion, so both are false. Neither is equivalent to the original.

Therefore III and IV only are equivalent, choice B.
